newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean mining improves environmental stand.
newsitem.headline: Chilean mining improves environmental stand.

text.p: After years of neglect and indifference, Chilean mining firms are starting to pay more attention to environmental standards and bring operations in line with those in the rest of the world, experts said on Tuesday.

Laxer environmental standards are becoming a less important factor in drawing foreign investment to Chile from the United States, Canada and other countries with stricter green laws, they told a conference on environmental law and mining.

"The environment is something that no one in our country ever worried about or thought about at all, at least not in the early years," said Jose Antonio Urrutia, a specialist in environmental law and mining at the University of Chile.
"It was something no one cared about or spoke about (in the mining industry)," he told the conference.

Mining pollution has become a major issue in Chile, with state copper firm Codelco forced to spend heavily on cutting air pollution and mines accused of causing widespread water pollution. Contamination of the Loa river near Chuquicamata has become front-page news.

Urrutia said a change began in 1992 at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, when Chile signed various environmental treaties, and that Chile was now in the "harmonization process" of bringing its legislation and industrial standards up to par with the rest of the world.

Wade Martin of the Colorado School of Mines in the United States said looser environmental standards had been only a minor factor in drawing mining investment away from North America and into developing countries like Chile.

But figures on mining exploration could be read to support either conclusion, he said. On one hand, exploration in the United States, Canada and Australia combined has fallen to about 35-40 percent today from 70 percent in 1990 as a portion of worldwide exploration, he said.
"But in constant dollar terms, it's held roughly steady in the United States," said Martin. Canada has seen some decline, he said.

"The question then becomes, would that money have stayed (in the United States) if we hadn't had such cumbersome environmental laws?" he said. "I think it's a factor but only a minor factor" in transfer of investment into developing countries like Chile, he said.

Much of the pressure on companies to clean up their acts is coming from their own stockholders, especially in the case of big foreign companies operating in northern Chile's copper belt, speakers said.

Environmental impact statements and studies are now the rule for even small Chilean mining firms, said University of Chile specialist Jose Miguel Sanchez. But enforcement of air and water standards is still patchy, speakers said.
